concept.name: Long-short ratio
concept.definition: The long-short ratio is the proportion of long to short positioning in a derivatives market — reported by exchanges either by account count or by position size — used as a sentiment and crowding gauge.
concept.intuition: It is the seating chart of the derivatives arena: how many traders are on the bullish side versus the bearish side, and how lopsided the crowd has become.
concept.mechanics: Computed as longs / shorts; e.g. a BTCUSDT ratio of 1.8145 means 1.81 long positions per short (64.5% long, 35.5% short). Venues publish variants: all accounts, top-trader positions (dollar-weighted) and top-trader accounts (count-weighted), which can diverge usefully when whales lean one way and the crowd the other. Extreme readings are often used contrarian.
concept.formula: Long/short ratio = number (or size) of long positions / number (or size) of short positions.
concept.failure_modes: The ratio says nothing about leverage size per account (count-based) or hedged books — a 'long' account may be hedged short elsewhere; venue-specific populations (retail-heavy Binance vs institutional CME) make cross-venue comparison meaningless.
concept.misconceptions: A high ratio is not a bullish signal to follow — extreme one-sidedness historically precedes squeezes in the opposite direction (contrarian use). Account-count ratios also don't measure conviction; one whale can outweigh thousands of minnows in notional terms.
concept.example: Binance BTCUSDT top-trader ratio at 2.5 (dollar-weighted) with funding at +0.05% signals crowded, leveraged longs — a setup where a small dip can trigger outsized long liquidations.
